title: On the Spectral Geometry of Cross-Modal Representations: A Functional Map Diagnostic for Multimodal Alignment
abstract: We study cross-modal alignment between independently pretrained vision (DINOv2) and language (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) encoders using the functional map framework from computational geometry, which represents correspondence between representation manifolds as a compact linear operator between graph Laplacian eigenbases. While the framework underperforms Procrustes alignment and relative representations for cross-modal retrieval across all supervision budgets, it reveals a structural property of multimodal representations. We find that the Laplacian eigenvalue spectra of the two encoders are quantitatively similar (normalized spectral distance 0.043), indicating that independently trained models develop manifolds of comparable intrinsic complexity. However, the functional map exhibits near-zero diagonal dominance (mean below 0.05) and large orthogonality error (70.15), showing that the eigenvector bases are effectively unaligned. We term this decoupling the spectral complexity--orientation gap: models converge in how much structure they capture but not in how they organize it. This gap defines a boundary condition for spectral alignment methods and motivates three diagnostic quantities : diagonal dominance, orthogonality deviation, and Laplacian commutativity error for characterizing cross-modal representation compatibility.

title: ComBench: A Repo-level Real-world Benchmark for Compilation Error Repair
abstract: Compilation errors pose pervasive and critical challenges in software development, significantly hindering productivity. Therefore, Automated Compilation Error Repair (ACER) techniques are proposed to mitigate these issues. Despite recent advancements in ACER, its real-world performance remains poorly evaluated. This can be largely attributed to the limitations of existing benchmarks, \ie decontextualized single-file data, lack of authentic source diversity, and biased local task modeling that ignores crucial repository-level complexities. To bridge this critical gap, we propose ComBench, the first repository-level, reproducible real-world benchmark for C/C++ compilation error repair. ComBench is constructed through a novel, automated framework that systematically mines real-world failures from the GitHub CI histories of large-scale open-source projects. Our framework contributes techniques for the high-precision identification of ground-truth repair patches from complex version histories and a high-fidelity mechanism for reproducing the original, ephemeral build environments. To ensure data quality, all samples in ComBench are execution-verified -- guaranteeing reproducible failures and build success with ground-truth patches. Using ComBench, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 12 modern LLMs under both direct and agent-based repair settings. Our experiments reveal a significant gap between a model's ability to achieve syntactic correctness (a 73% success rate for GPT-5) and its ability to ensure semantic correctness (only 41% of its patches are valid). We also find that different models exhibit distinct specializations for different error types. ComBench provides a robust and realistic platform to guide the future development of ACER techniques capable of addressing the complexities of modern software development.

title: ADAPTIVE ANALYTICS PIPELINES FOR CONCEPT DRIFT IN HIGH- FREQUENCY BIG DATA ENVIRONMENTS
abstract: ABSTRACT Big data systems with high frequency and large scale generate dynamic and constantly evolving data streams that create a problem for traditional machine learning models due to concept drift. Adaptive analytics pipelines are discussed in this paper, and identify and respond to changing data distributions in real time. It talks about the drift types, pipeline design and adaptation means, such as online learning and ensemble techniques. Other important issues addressed in the study are the latency, scalability, and computational cost. The findings focus on the importance of automated, scalable and real-time adaptive systems to guarantee model accuracy and reliability of decisions in dynamic data-driven environments. Keywords: Concept drift, Big data, Real-time analytics, Machine learning, Streaming data.

title: Why My T-1000 Needs to Borrow My TI-81: The Calculator Paradox in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models do not compute mathematical results; they predict what mathematical results look like. This paper identifies a failure mode we term the Calculator Paradox: LLMs fail most dangerously not on overtly difficult mathematical problems but on problems that appear non-mathematical yet require genuine computation—temporal calculations, implicit comparisons, and linguistically simple quantitative assertions where neither party expects failure. We present evidence from a live research session and a controlled demonstration experiment, including a phrasing ablation that isolates perceived difficulty as a causal variable. We introduce a two-component measure of implicit computation density—C₁ (operation density) and C₂ (decision-boundary sensitivity)—to characterize the hidden quantitative load carried by natural-language assertions and its downstream brittleness. We argue that the critical vulnerability is the model’s inability to distinguish arithmetic it can perform from arithmetic it merely pattern-matches: the threshold judgment itself constitutes the bug. We propose a default-to-verification architecture with progressive verification tiers, inverting the standard tool-invocation paradigm. We distinguish the Calculator Paradox from hallucination as a separate failure type and situate it within a unified framework of metacognitive collapse in autoregressive systems, encompassing the author’s prior analyses of Novelty Blindness, the Temporal Gap in LLM Memory Systems, and the AI Depth Asymmetry.Keywords: large language models, arithmetic reasoning, tool use, computational co-processors, calculator paradox, token prediction, threshold judgment, implicit computation density, metacognitive collapse, default-to-verification

title: Geometric Intelligence Theory Case Study Novel, Volume 11 : The Inverse Function of the Westerlies
abstract: About This Volume This book is a case study — written in the form of a novel — illustrating the practical application of the Geometric Intelligence (GI) theoretical framework developed in Volumes 1 and 2 of the series. As of March 2026, every mathematical theorem, artificial intelligence technique, cryptographic method, and information technology employed here reflects work that actually exists. GI Theory, Volume 1: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19140530 https://zenn.dev/etalecohomology/books/9f680ca9dddf2a GI Theory, Volume 2: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19158228 The challenges that arise when applying GI Theory to real industry practice differ substantially from one sector to the next. Data collection, entity resolution, harmonisation of temporal and categorical granularities, and the statistical normalisation required to make measurements expressed in different units mutually comparable — none of these admit a universal solution. The structure of a dataset is inseparable from the structure of the industry that produced it, and no one-size-fits-all preprocessing pipeline spans industries. For this reason, the series issues a dedicated case study for each sector. Previous volumes have addressed textile manufacturing, general construction, and semiconductor fabrication. This volume turns to commercial aviation. The Story and Why This Setting Was Chosen The year is 2031. Japan's National Security Secretariat assigns Tenshō Air a task: transport a specific diplomatic consignment to London Heathrow within seventy-two hours. The problem is that three independent airspace restrictions have closed every conventional route between Tokyo and London. The first: Russia's revocation of Siberian overflight permits for European, Japanese, and Canadian carriers — a retaliatory measure sustained since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The second: China's progressive tightening of overflight procedures across its FIRs, driven by escalating tension over the Taiwan Strait. The third: the Houthi movement's surface-to-air missile and drone threat along the Red Sea coast, which has made the traditional southern routing untenable for commercial aircraft since 2023. No standard routing survives the simultaneous application of all three constraints. The only remaining option is a non-standard polar routing through the Arctic Ocean. This scenario is not imagined. It reflects the geopolitical reality of the present day. Article 1 of the 1944 Chicago Convention declares that every state possesses complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory; Article 9 authorises the immediate prohibition of flight over any part of that territory in an emergency. The legal framework has been unchanged for nearly eighty years. What has changed is the environment in which it operates: the range of actors exercising airspace sovereignty has expanded from states to non-state entities such as the Houthis; airspace closure has been normalised as a tool of political retaliation; and threats now arrive from outside the treaty framework entirely. The compound effect of these three shifts has qualitatively altered the constraints that commercial carriers face in maintaining continuous operations. This book encodes that complexity in the language of algebraic topology: when three independent restricted zones are superimposed on the flight domain B, they punch three holes into it, rendering the first cohomology group H¹(B, F) non-trivial. No standard geodesic exists in such a space. The story of this novel is the story of finding — and flying — one anyway. The central question the book pursues is whether a mathematical framework can serve as a working instrument for the people who must make decisions on the flight deck, under real constraints, in real time. Applying GI Theory to Commercial Aviation: Characteristics and Challenges The aviation dataset and its distinguishing properties The most consequential difference between aviation data and the data encountered in manufacturing or maritime applications is this: in aviation, the wind renders the metric asymmetric. In most industries, environmental factors enter the model as exogenous noise. In aviation, the same city-pair flown eastbound and westbound differs by two to three hours in block time. Distance, in the operational sense, has lost its symmetry — and a standard Riemannian metric, which assigns the same length to a path regardless of direction, cannot accurately represent this. The metric employed throughout this volume is the Randers metric F = α + β, a special case of the Finsler metric class. Here α is the background Riemannian metric — distance in still air — and β is a 1-form encoding the jet stream's contribution, a term that changes sign with flight direction. Their sum F captures the directional asymmetry of actual flight. The Randers metric is provably equivalent to Zermelo's navigation problem, the classical formulation of time-optimal navigation in the presence of wind, making it the natural mathematical language for commercial aviation route design. A further property distinguishes aviation data from other sectors. Every commercial aircraft continuously broadcasts its GPS-derived position, speed, and altitude on the ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) system. This volume uses 23,847 ADS-B records covering all Tokyo–London flights over a five-year period. Unlike production-line data from a factory or voyage logs from a ship, ADS-B records contain direct observations of the wind vector: the difference between true airspeed (TAS) and ground speed (GS) at each moment is, by definition, the wind acting on the aircraft. This is a property unique to aviation. It means the Randers β-term can be learned from actual flight data, without dependence on external meteorological forecasts. Satisfying the three conditions of Proposition 1.1 with aviation data GI Theory Volume 1, Proposition 1.1, requires three conditions to be satisfied before a variational autoencoder (VAE) can be used to construct a differentiable manifold. Condition (i): C³ smoothness of the VAE decoder. The choice of activation function is decisive. Aviation manifold data involves abrupt transitions in altitude, speed, and attitude; the ReLU activation is inadmissible here because its subgradient at zero introduces a discontinuity in the first derivative, making the second derivatives required for the Christoffel symbols undefined. All layers use the hyperbolic tangent (tanh), which is C∞, guaranteeing the continuity the geodesic equation demands. Condition (ii): Full rank of the Jacobian. After training, the singular value decomposition of the decoder's Jacobian was computed. The minimum singular value of 0.312 confirmed full rank. A K-nearest-neighbour preservation rate of 0.891 — above the 0.85 target — verified that the latent space geometry faithfully reflects the manifold structure of the actual flight data. Condition (iii): The Randers condition ‖β‖_α < 1. This is mathematically equivalent to the physical requirement that wind speed not exceed the aircraft's true airspeed. For a Boeing 787-9 cruising at approximately 250 m/s (Mach 0.85), the North Pacific jet stream typically runs between 50 and 100 m/s, giving a ratio of around 0.40. The condition was satisfied throughout the flight; the measured values were 0.38 at departure and a maximum of 0.56 in flight. A Riemannian fallback — automatically triggered if the β-norm exceeds 0.65, the point at which the theoretical stability of the time-varying Finsler metric is no longer guaranteed — was incorporated into the system design from the outset. Designing openly around the limits of the theory, rather than concealing them, is itself a requirement of aviation safety standards. In addition, a dual-source data architecture — cross-referencing GFS/ECMWF forecast models against real-time ADS-B measurements — held β-term estimation error within ±0.04. When communications were severed during the eleven-minute solar-flare blackout over the Arctic Ocean, the onboard Embodied Agents continued updating the metric autonomously from the last known state, without any dependence on ground contact. A Message to Readers Late in the story, a young software engineer named Kaito says: "I've worked hard to understand mathematics, physics, and programming. But since joining this operation, I've come to think I need to get serious about international politics and law as well." His words crystallise something that runs throughout the book: the practitioner of GI Theory must be a person who can stand at the intersection of several different disciplines simultaneously. Deploying GI Theory in commercial aviation requires all of the following, at once. Mathematical knowledge — Finsler geometry (the Randers metric, the Chern connection, geodesic equations), algebraic topology (cohomology groups, zigzag persistence), optimal control theory (the Pontryagin maximum principle, adjoint variables), and information geometry (the Fisher information metric, VAE pullback metrics) — not as separate subjects but as a single connected system. Every piece of mathematics in this book is taught at the graduate level in at least one leading university. No curriculum anywhere in the world, as of 2026, teaches all of them as an integrated whole. Engineering and AI implementation — architecture design satisfying the C³ condition, a numerical Finsler geodesic solver fast enough to recompute in approximately forty seconds, the design and communication protocols for fourteen parallel AI Agents, the combination of formal verification (Lean 4) with zero-knowledge machine learning (ZKML) for post-flight proof generation. Theory that cannot be made to run is not yet complete.
